title: Daniel in the Lions' Den
overview: Jealous officials trick a king into making Daniel's daily prayer a crime, and he is thrown to the lions but comes out unharmed.

parts.label: Rivals hunt for dirt (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Daniel, an exile from Judah who is now old, rises so high in the new government that jealous officials search his work for corruption and find none. Outside this book there is no clear historical record of a Darius the Mede, so who he was is still debated.

parts.label: A law that cannot be undone (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: The officials flatter the king into banning prayer to anyone but him for thirty days, knowing Daniel will not stop praying to his God. Once signed, the law is said to be unchangeable under Persian custom, an idea also found in the book of Esther, so the king's own word becomes the trap.

parts.label: Daniel prays as before (vv. 10-15)
parts.note: Daniel keeps praying three times a day facing Jerusalem, home of the destroyed temple, neither hiding nor making a show of protest. The king sees he has been played and spends the day looking for a way out that his own law will not allow.

parts.label: A night with the lions (vv. 16-23)
parts.note: Daniel is put in a pit sealed with a stone and with the rings of the king and his nobles, so no one could change his fate, and at dawn he says God's angel shut the lions' mouths. Christians have often read the sealed stone and the morning rescue as pointing ahead to Jesus' sealed tomb and resurrection.

parts.label: The accusers' fate (v. 24)
parts.note: The king throws the accusers into the den with their wives and children, and the lions kill them all at once. Punishing whole families was a known practice in ancient empires, and the text reports it without comment, which many readers find deeply troubling.

parts.label: The king honors Daniel's God (vv. 25-28)
parts.note: Darius orders his empire to respect Daniel's God, whose kingdom, he says, will never end, echoing the book's theme that human empires fall while God's rule lasts. Daniel ends the chapter still serving, now under Cyrus, the Persian king who later let exiles return home.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter records events as they happened in the Persian period or is a story shaped later, possibly during persecution in the second century BC, to encourage faithful Jews living under hostile rulers.
think: Is there anything you would keep doing even if a law or someone in power made it costly, and what makes it worth that to you?
